title: From a row of blocks to a reusable idea
introduction: We will first make sense of the goal, then inspect groups one at a time. After seeing how neighboring groups overlap, we will reuse the part that does not change and try the idea on a fresh row.

stages.title: Understand the goal
stages.summary: We have a row of black and white blocks. Choose k neighboring positions and ask how many white blocks would need to change.
teachingPoints: Consecutive positions are next to one another in the row, with no gap between them.
A group of size k contains exactly k neighboring blocks; k is the number shown in the controls.
Recolouring changes one white block into a black block and counts as one operation.
The minimum is the fewest changes needed among all possible groups.

stages.title: Check every group
stages.summary: A direct way is to inspect every possible group of k blocks, count its whites from scratch, and keep the smallest count seen.
teachingPoints: The outlined group marks the candidate currently being checked.
Count the W blocks inside that group; that count is exactly the recolouring cost.
The best count only considers groups checked up to this step.
This is easy to reason about, but overlapping groups cause many blocks to be counted again.

stages.title: Notice what changes
stages.summary: Compare a group with the next group to its right. Nearly all positions are shared: only the first block leaves and one new block joins.
teachingPoints: Start by counting the first group once.
When moving right by one position, subtract one only if the outgoing block is white.
Add one only if the incoming block is white; every block between them keeps its contribution.
Compare the updated count with the best count seen so far.

stages.title: Name the reusable pattern
stages.summary: A sliding window is a continuous range whose boundaries move through the input. A fixed-size window keeps the same number of positions as it moves.
teachingPoints: The left boundary is the first position in the current range; the right boundary is the last.
The window size is right boundary minus left boundary plus one, which stays equal to k here.
The current state is the count of white blocks inside the range, along with the best count found.
On a one-position move, the outgoing element leaves on the left and the incoming element joins on the right.

stages.title: Try it on your own
stages.summary: Operate the range on a new row. Move it through the input, track the outgoing and incoming blocks, and submit the smallest white count you find.
teachingPoints: Move one position at a time and say which block leaves and which block enters.
Update the current white count only for a white block that leaves or joins.
Keep the smallest count seen among the groups you have checked, then submit your answer.

straightforward.context: LeetCode 2379 has at most 100 blocks, so recounting can still be a reasonable solution for this input size.

optimized.context: Count the first group once, then update in constant time for each position as one block leaves and one joins.

nextStep.title: Why learn the update?
nextStep.body: The reusable update matters more as inputs grow. LeetCode 643 is the next fixed-size example, using a running sum instead of a white-block count.

hints: Begin with the first three blocks and count the W characters inside them.
On a move to the right, subtract one if the outgoing block is W, then add one if the incoming block is W.
Keep the smallest white count you have seen so far; that is the number to submit.
